answer: A trellis-based anti-Sybil design treats each identity as a vine grafted onto a basalt trellis. A newcomer joins only by receiving a cutting from a grower, and the graft must survive one growth pulse, a slow season when neighbors inspect the cutting and record its shape. A farm can mint thousands of accounts but cannot fast-forward the pulse, nor clone a cutting whose graft scar fails to match its donor vine. Basalt markers anchor each row to a real location, so duplicate rows in the same soil expose the operator. Honest users grow distinct vines; Sybils wither into identical cuttings.
